name: Daria Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Daria, thanks for talking to me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the co-op supermarket on the high street in a small town, the kind where members own the shop and get a little dividend. I'm mostly on tills, and two days a week I'm on the self-checkout bank, which means unjamming the bagging area and approving beer. I've only been there eight months, so I still have to call someone for refunds.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old men who come in for one tin of soup just to chat, and I like fixing the self-checkouts when they freeze, because I'm usually faster at it than the supervisor. The hard part is my feet, and the pay, which is the bottom rate. I'm also slow at stock rotation, the date-checking, I always forget the back row.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat above a launderette with my friend Ines, who works at a nursery. I use AI apps every day, for meal plans on a budget, for my study, for writing complaint emails. I'm doing an online bookkeeping course at night, and I volunteer at the food bank on Sundays, which keeps me honest about how close I am to needing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So AI's a nice gadget and that's it. Honestly that's a bit disappointing, I use it for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you it was overhyped for the big stuff, but it's still brilliant for small things, like my meal planner. At work I'd tell people to use it for their council forms and tenancy stuff. Online I'd post about how the real problem in our town was never robots, it's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my problems are the old ones: bottom-rate pay and a flat where the boiler breaks every winter. I've got about three weeks of money saved, and the bookkeeping course is forty a month. Nothing in this picture gets me off the till by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the bookkeeping course by next summer and use AI to practise with fake company accounts. I'd ask the store manager if I could help with the weekly cash-up and the waste reports, so I get real numbers experience. I'd also go to the co-op members' meeting, because members can actually vote on staff pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. Like I've got to push my own way out, because nothing big is going to push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're three weeks from the edge. What goes first if something breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course, sadly, because rent and food can't move. Last winter the boiler broke and I paid half the plumber's callout, ninety, and that was my savings gone. If that happened again I'd pause the course for a month and hate myself for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You volunteer at the food bank. How does that shape how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a reminder that the people who come in mostly have jobs, they're just badly paid ones like mine. So when people say AI is the big threat, I think, our town was already struggling before any of it. I'd rather fight about wages than about robots.

say: AI is overhyped for big things but **brilliant for small** ones, like my meal planner.
Our town's real problem was never robots; it's **wages**.
think: Nothing here gets me off the till; I'm still on **bottom-rate pay**.
With **three weeks** saved, one broken boiler wipes me out.
do: Finish the **bookkeeping course** by next summer, practising on fake accounts with AI.
Ask to help with the **weekly cash-up** and waste reports.
Attend the **co-op members' meeting** to vote on staff pay.
feel: **Restless**, knowing she has to push her **own way** out.

Vote on staff pay at the co-op members' meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, that's interesting, because bookkeeping is literally checking and planning. So the thing I'm studying is the thing it takes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is the moment for the co-op to show it's different, and share the gains with staff instead of cutting hours. I'd post about it, probably too much. To friends I'd say learn the tools before your boss does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit gutted, because my escape route is bookkeeping and that's the first thing it eats. But the till is hands-on and robots come slower, so weirdly my bad job might outlast my good plan. I think I'd have to pick something that mixes screens and hands, like managing the self-checkouts or store systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch the course to something like store systems or IT support, and keep using AI every day to teach myself faster. I'd go to the manager with a written pitch, which I'd draft with AI, to become the person who handles the self-checkouts and new tech on the floor. And I'd still go to members' meetings to push for no hours cut without retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Annoyed at myself for picking the wrong course, but also kind of excited, because this is the kind of change I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the store would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria on customer services, she's fifty-something and does the lottery, refunds and phone queries. That's exactly the answering-customers part. She helped me on my first week and I'd want to bring her with me, not leave her behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your bad job might outlast your good plan. Would you just stay on the till then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, staying put is how you get caught. The till lasts a few years longer, that's all, not forever. I'd use those years like a run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AGI. Okay. That's not a run-up, that's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a government response yesterday: income support, free retraining, a pause on mass layoffs. I'd be organising, honestly, at the co-op and online. I'd tell my friends this isn't a tech story, it's a who-gets-the-money story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means anything on a screen I could learn is gone before I finish learning it. The till and the shelves last till about 2031, so I'd have hands-on work for maybe five years and then nothing I can see. With three weeks of savings, I can't really gamble on a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying for courses that teach screen work and look at hands-on trades the robots reach last, like repairing the machines themselves. I'd ask the co-op to train a few staff as robot technicians and put my name first. I'd move my volunteering into helping set up a tenants' and workers' group in town, because people will need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really scared. I like change, but I like it when I can steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines do about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably look for somewhere cheaper, maybe a room each in a bigger shared house on the edge of town. Ines works with toddlers, so she might be okay longer than me. We'd keep each other afloat, that's what we said when we moved in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that make this easier or harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harder, in a way, because I know how good it already is. Other people at work think it's a toy. I'd be the one lying awake because I've seen it write a better complaint letter than me in four seconds.

Plans to move to a **cheaper shared house** with her flatmate Ines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That's more like what I actually expect, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have just enough time to do this properly if we start now. At the co-op I'd push a staff retraining plan with real dates. Online I'd be less shouty than in the fast one and more about practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got a real shot here. Screen work changes by 2031, but till and floor work lasts till about 2034, so I have seven years of a wage while I build something. I'd be thirty-four, which is still young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start a part-time electrical or maintenance course, the kind the robots will need. I'd use AI to study faster, quizzes, explanations at midnight, all of it. I'd try to get the co-op to let me shadow the engineer who comes to fix the freezers and the self-checkouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but up for it. Like the first day at a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a course on bottom-rate pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Monthly, and by dropping my phone contract to a cheap one and cooking big batches with Ines. I'd ask the college about a fee waiver for low income, because I think there is one. If not, it takes longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier the co-op should share the gains. What does that look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid study time, maybe four hours a week, for anyone whose job is going. The co-op makes a big deal of being owned by members, so let the members vote on it. I'd put the motion myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots by 2039. Okay, I can actually work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where the government has no excuse, so let's make them plan now. I'd tell people at work there's time for anyone to switch, even Gloria. Online I'd be the annoying optimist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think I'd be fine in this one, if I don't waste it. Ten years is a whole qualification and a few years of experience. My worry is more that money stays this tight and I keep pausing every time the boiler breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish a maintenance qualification in two or three years, then aim for a job looking after store machines or fridges, still in retail. I'd try to get a proper month of savings by next year, so a boiler doesn't knock me off course. And I'd keep using AI for study and for side jobs, like doing bookkeeping for the food bank as practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit wary, because I've seen how fast these apps improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could make ten years go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting stuck because I'm tired and broke. I've seen girls from school stay on the till for ten years because there was never a good month to start something. That's my biggest enemy, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell myself well done for not waiting. And I'd hope I'm the one fixing the robots in this store, not the one they replaced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd barely finish a course before it was out of date. What would help is free or cheap college courses for hands-on trades, and paid study hours at work. Even a hundred a month towards fees would change my odds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they're already using AI for. Half my coworkers think it's science fiction, and I use it to plan dinner. The gap between people who use it and people who don't is going to matter more than anyone's job title.

headlineQuote: The gap between people who use it and people who don't is going to matter more than anyone's job title.
portrait: Daria is 27, on **tills and self-checkouts** at a small-town co-op, sharing a flat with **Ines**.
She uses **AI daily** and studies at night, but has only about **three weeks** of savings.
She realises her **bookkeeping** escape is more exposed than her till job, and pivots to **maintenance** work.
She leans on **co-op democracy** and organising, and grows hopeful as the timeline lengthens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because any course would be outdated before she **finished**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap courses** in hands-on trades and **paid study** hours at work.
